q4a.caption: Diagram 1 — the carbon-tax dimension from €0 to €140: the seven ideal points, the status quo (€50), the median (France, €80), the agenda setter (FR) and the veto player (HU).

q4c.caption: Diagram 2 — SQ = €50. Winset of the status quo (€30–€90) and Hungary’s acceptance set (€0–€50, everything within €30 of its ideal). The overlap is €30–€50, so France’s best feasible proposal is €50: no change.

q4d.caption: Diagram 3 — SQ = €20 (Hungary’s ideal point). Almost everyone prefers a higher tax, but Hungary accepts only €20 itself, so the veto freezes policy at €20.

q4e.caption: Diagram 4 — SQ = €35. The winset runs upward from €35; Hungary accepts €5–€35 (within €15 of its ideal). The overlap is the single point €35, so the status quo stands.

q5a1.caption: Diagram 5 — the 100×100 policy space with the three blocs’ ideal points and the status quo at (40,40). The ideal points form a proper triangle (sides ≈ 46, 35 and 56), not a line.

q5b1.caption: Diagram 6 — each bloc’s indifference curve through SQ is a circle centred on its ideal point; the interior is what that bloc prefers to SQ. The winset of SQ is the region covered by at least two circles — it is far from empty. (45,55) is inside the Environmental and Tech circles and so beats SQ; (50,50), (65,35) and (35,65) do not.

q5c1.caption: Diagram 7 — Environmental has a veto: only points inside its circle through SQ are acceptable. Tech, as agenda setter, proposes the acceptable point closest to its own ideal — where the Tech–Environmental line meets the circle, about (40,58) (the key rounds this to (43,58)).

q5d1.caption: Diagram 8 — two veto players (Environmental and Skeptic): the feasible set is the lens where their two circles overlap. The contract curve — the Pareto-efficient bargains between the two — is the segment joining their ideal points; inside the lens it is the only place an agenda setter can go. Because both circles pass through SQ, the lens is the thin sliver between SQ and the circles’ second crossing, and only a short stretch of the contract curve lies inside it; Tech picks its end nearest (30,60), about (42,34). (The key’s rough figure of (35,42) lies just outside the lens.)

q5d2.caption: Diagram 8 (again) — the contract curve through the lens: the straight segment between the Environmental and Skeptic ideal points, where their indifference curves are tangent to one another.

q5e1.caption: Diagram 9 — three veto players: only points inside all three circles are feasible. With these coordinates SQ (40,40) lies inside the triangle of ideal points, so it is already Pareto-efficient and the three discs touch only at SQ: no proposal makes all three blocs better off, and policy cannot move at all. (The key’s estimate of a small region around (38,42) is a rough approximation; the drawing uses the exact coordinates.)

q5f1.caption: Diagram 10 — the one-dimensional version (renewable subsidies only): Skeptic €25, Tech €30, Environmental €75, SQ €40. Tech is the median voter and can carry €30 with Skeptic’s support.

q6a.caption: Diagram 11 — closed rule. Outcome as a function of the committee’s ideal point C: flat at SQ for C below SQ; equal to C (the committee gets its ideal) as long as the floor median prefers it to SQ, i.e. up to 2M − SQ; flat at 2M − SQ — the point where the median is indifferent to SQ — for any committee further out. The key describes the same kinked shape.

q6b.caption: Diagram 12 — open rule. Whatever the committee proposes is amended to the floor median: the equilibrium is a horizontal line at M.

q6c.caption: Diagram 13 — zero-based budgeting (reversion point 0) added as a dashed line. Closed rule: the median now compares every proposal with 0, so the committee gets its ideal up to 2M and 2M beyond — more than under the old reversion point. Open rule: still M.
Diagram 13b — open rule with ZB = 0: the reversion point is irrelevant because the floor median can always amend to M.

q10a.caption: Diagram 14 — Downsian convergence: with a single-peaked, normally distributed electorate, both vote-maximising parties locate at the median voter’s position (50).
